title: EEG hyperscanning using a single-person EEG recording setup
author: Douglas, Tremblay, et al.
materials: 64-electrode silver-silver chloride coated active ActiCap active electrodes
Brain Products actiCHamp 64 channel EEG amplifier
ActiCap ground distributor and two ground electrodes
Electrolyte gel compatible with the EEG system
Double-sided circular medical adhesives for electrodes

EEG system and accessories:•64-electrode silver-silver chloride coated active ActiCap active electrodes (Brain Products, Gilching, Germany), provided as two bundles of 32 electrodes each•4 silver-silver chloride disk electrodes (for electrooculogram — EOG — monitoring)•Brain Products actiCHamp 64 channel EEG amplifier (Brain Products)•StimTrak device (Brain Products)•ActiCap ground distributor and two ground electrodes (Brain Products)•2 BIP2AUX adapters (Brain Products)•2 flexible fabric EEG caps

EEG consumables:•Electrolyte gel compatible with the EEG system (e.g., Brain Products’ SuperVisc)•Exfoliating skin prep gel (e.g., Nuprep; Weaver and Company, Aurora, USA)•Double-sided circular medical adhesives for electrodes•Plastic electrode washers

Supporting Technology Requirements:•Computer running Windows operating system, for recording EEG, with the following software installed:○PyCorder recording software (Brain Products)•Computer for data analysis, with the following software installed:○Praat version 6.1.42 [13]○Python version 3.6 or higher○MNE-Python package and associated dependencies (see https://mne.tools/) [14]

Fig. 2 shows the configuration of EEG recording equipment. Details of the setup and procedure are below.Fig. 2A diagram of the EEG hyperscanning setup. This uses a single, 64-channel EEG amplifier which takes as input two separate bundles of 32 electrodes each. For hyperscanning, one bundle of 32 electrodes is placed on each participant's head. Ground electrodes placed on the scalp of each participant are connected to a ground distributor device (Brain Products) that connects to the ground input on the amplifier. EOG is captured using a bipolar pair of electrodes placed around each participant's eyes, which connect to AUX ports on the amplifier via Brain Products BIP2AUX devices. Audio is recorded from both participants using the microphone built into the StimTrak device (Brain Products), which is connected to the EEG amplifier. As a result, EEG from two participants, as well as audio during the study, are recorded synchronously through a single amplifier and recording computer, to a single data file.Fig 2

The results we present in this paper are from an initial pilot experiment that led to the design an execution of two experiments, each involving 40 participants. In those experiments we used a scripted conversation, rather than free conversation, to provide more consistency in the number and identity of content words for which ERPs were derived. Preliminary results of these have been reported [19,20], and a manuscript is currently in preparation, but in short these experiments yielded robust N400 effects consistent with our demonstration here, and past single-participant research. Furthermore, Fjaellingsdal and colleagues recently [21] demonstrated that ERP responses (including the N400 ERP) occurred in participants equipped with a non-hyperscanning EEG setup who engaged in a spontaneous word-by-word sentence construction task with a non-EEG equipped confederate. A similar study could easily be conducted using the methods outlined in this paper where both people involved undergo EEG and are participants to examine if these findings hold out in slightly less controlled circumstances. Another single participant study examined the differences between how adults and infants processed the same mother-infant interaction [22]. There were ERP differences in processing contingent and non-contingent speech when listening to a 20-minute recording of a naturalistic free conversational interaction of a mother and her baby between the infants and adults. This indicates that there may be differences in cognitive processing across the life span when viewing the same interaction as infants displayed different ERP responses in comparison to the adult control group. Using the methodology outlined here, with only minor adaptations, would allow the examination and recording of infants and parent pairings while they themselves are engaged in conversational interactions, rather than being limited to examining only the outside observer role responses to these interactions.

steps.title: Configure EEG Recording Software
steps.instruction: Set up the PyCorder recording configuration to ensure channels are correctly labeled for each participant.

substeps.instruction: Label channels 1–32 and the first bipolar EOG channel with the prefix 'P1_'.
Label channels 33–64 and the second bipolar channel with the prefix 'P2_'.
Set the sampling rate to 10,000 Hz to ensure audio intelligibility.

steps.title: Prepare Participant Skin
steps.instruction: Prepare the skin at electrode placement sites to ensure low impedance.

substeps.instruction: Measure participants' heads to determine the correct EEG cap size.
Apply exfoliating skin prep gel (e.g., Nuprep) to the periorbital region (lateral to left eyebrow and below the left eye), the left and right masseter regions, and both sides of the larynx.

steps.title: Apply EEG Caps and Electrodes
steps.instruction: Fit the EEG caps and attach the necessary electrodes for scalp, ground, and EMG monitoring.

substeps.instruction: Place the EEG cap on each participant and tighten the chin strap for stability.
Attach a ground electrode to each cap and connect them to the ground distributor, then plug the distributor into the EEG system ground connector.

Apply EMG electrodes using double-sided circular medical adhesives: place electrodes 1 and 2 from each 32-electrode bundle on the face (masseters) and electrodes 17 and 18 from each bundle on either side of the larynx.
Attach the remaining 28 electrodes of each bundle to the cap according to the 10-10 System montage.
Assign electrode bundle 1–32 to Participant 1 and bundle 33–64 to Participant 2.

steps.title: Ensure Electrode Connection and Impedance
steps.instruction: Establish a high-quality electrical connection between the scalp and electrodes.

substeps.instruction: Inject electrolyte gel (e.g., SuperVisc) into the gap between the electrode and scalp using a blunt-tipped syringe, rubbing gently with the tip.
Plug electrodes into the amplifier and load the recording montage in PyCorder.
Perform an impedance check; ensure ground electrodes are lowered as much as possible first.
Verify all electrodes have an impedance level below 25 kOhm, adding gel and rubbing the area if necessary.

steps.title: Configure StimTrak Audio Device
steps.instruction: Set up the StimTrak device to record audio as an auxiliary EEG channel.

substeps.instruction: Install freshly charged batteries in the StimTrak device.
Set the Trigger Level to 1 V and the Gain dial to 'Mic'.
Connect the Signal Out port of the StimTrak to the AUX 1 port on the actiCHamp amplifier.
Verify audio recording in PyCorder by checking the auxiliary channel at 10,000 Hz and performing a test (e.g., speaking and clapping).

steps.title: Acquire EEG and Audio Data
steps.instruction: Record the simultaneous EEG and audio data during the conversational task.

substeps.instruction: Start the recording in PyCorder.
Have participants engage in the experimental task (e.g., scripted or free conversation).
Stop the recording upon task completion and remove electrodes and gel from participants.

steps.title: Extract Audio and Preprocess Raw Data
steps.instruction: Separate the combined data stream into audio and EEG components using Python (MNE-Python and scipy).

substeps.instruction: Import the raw EEG data file and extract the audio recording to a WAV file using scipy.io.wavfile.write().
Concatenate raw data and remove accessory channels, leaving only EEG channels of interest.
Decimate the EEG data to 500 Hz.

steps.title: Identify Word Onsets
steps.instruction: Manually time-lock spoken words to the EEG recording using audio analysis software.

substeps.instruction: Load the extracted audio file into Praat software.
Identify the onset timing of words of interest (e.g., nouns) by viewing waveforms and listening to recordings.
Record the word identity, the speaker, and the onset timing (relative to the start of the file) in a spreadsheet.

steps.title: Generate Event Codes and Segment ERPs
steps.instruction: Convert audio onset timings into EEG trigger codes for ERP analysis.

substeps.instruction: Import the onset spreadsheet into MNE-Python to create a 3-column event array (timing, zero, and numeric code).
Assign numeric codes: '1' if the word was heard by Participant 1 (spoken by P2) and '2' if heard by Participant 2 (spoken by P1).
Segment the continuous data into ERP epochs from 200 ms prior to word onset to 1000 ms after.

steps.title: Perform EEG Signal Cleaning
steps.instruction: Apply filters and artifact removal to the segmented data.

substeps.instruction: Apply bandpass filtering: create one copy with a 1.0–20 Hz range (for ICA) and another with a 0.1–20 Hz range (for analysis).
Separate the dyadic recording into two individual datasets by removing the other participant's channels.
Re-reference each participant's data to the average of only the electrodes placed on their own scalp.
Baseline-correct epochs by subtracting the mean of the 200 ms preceding onset and remove linear trends.
Visually inspect epochs and manually remove excessively noisy trials.
Perform Independent Component Analysis (ICA) using the fastica algorithm to identify and remove ocular or EMG artifacts.
Perform a final baseline correction (mean of 200 ms pre-onset) and interpolate any removed bad scalp channels.
